name: Traditional Cuban
era: A living culture, formed over five centuries
line: Live close to music, neighbours, strong coffee and the art of making do.

quote.text: I am a sincere man from where the palm tree grows, and before I die I want to pour out the verses of my soul.

quotes.text: I grow a white rose, in July as in January, for the sincere friend who gives me his open hand.
To be educated is the only way to be free.
quotes.source: Maestros ambulantes, La América, New York, May 1884
Los factores humanos de la cubanidad, lecture at the University of Havana, 1939

quotes.text: To bad weather, a good face.
quotes.source: A Spanish-language saying in daily use in Cuba

words.meaning: To solve; to get by; to find a way
words.usage: The national verb. You resolve a spare part, a birthday cake, a lift to the next town.

words.meaning: To invent; to improvise a solution
words.usage: What you do when there is nothing to resolve with. A fan motor becomes a bicycle engine.

words.meaning: The time at the table after the meal is over
words.usage: Nobody gets up. Coffee comes. This is when the real conversation happens.

words.meaning: A small, strong, sweet coffee
words.usage: Offered to anyone who comes through the door, at any hour.

words.meaning: The root music of Cuba
words.usage: Born in the eastern hills from Spanish strings and African rhythm. Salsa is its grandchild.

words.meaning: The key rhythm; also the pair of sticks that play it
words.usage: Five strokes across two bars. Every other instrument fits itself to it.

words.meaning: The repeating groove of bass or conga; also a person’s swing
words.usage: To walk with tumbao is to walk as if the music were on.

words.meaning: The call-and-response section of a son
words.usage: The singer improvises, the chorus answers and the dancers take off.

words.meaning: Drum, song and dance of the Havana and Matanzas docks
words.usage: Three drums, sticks and voices. No relation to the ballroom dance of the same name.

words.meaning: A countryman; a small farmer
words.usage: The straw-hatted figure of the tobacco fields, and of the country music named after him.

words.meaning: A country party with music, roast pork and dancing
words.usage: Now used for any lively get-together.

words.meaning: A ten-line stanza
words.usage: The verse form of the Cuban countryside, sung and often made up on the spot.

words.meaning: A poet who improvises verses in song
words.usage: Two of them duel in décimas over a guitar, answering each other line for line.

words.meaning: A palm-thatched country house
words.usage: One of the Taíno words that survived the people who first spoke it, like hammock, canoe and tobacco.

words.meaning: A tobacco field
words.usage: The best lie in the red soil of Vuelta Abajo, in Pinar del Río.

words.meaning: A cigar roller
words.usage: A trade learned over years. Rollers tap their blades on the bench to applaud the reader.

words.meaning: The reader in a cigar factory
words.usage: Paid by the workers to read newspapers and novels aloud while they roll. The custom began in 1865.

words.meaning: Fresh-pressed sugar cane juice
words.usage: Sold from hand-cranked presses at the roadside, over ice.

words.meaning: A stew of many roots and meats
words.usage: Fernando Ortiz made it the image of the Cuban people: everything in one pot, still cooking.

words.meaning: Rice cooked together with beans
words.usage: Red beans in the east; with black beans the dish is called moros y cristianos.

words.meaning: The sea wall and promenade of Havana
words.usage: Eight kilometres of stone bench facing the Straits of Florida. The city’s living room.

words.meaning: A covered porch or arcade at the front of a house
words.usage: Where the rocking chairs are, and where the evening is spent.

words.meaning: A tenement built round a shared courtyard
words.usage: Many families, one yard, one tap. Rumba was born in them.

words.meaning: A carnival street band with dancers
words.usage: Each neighbourhood has its own, with its drums, lanterns and colours.

words.meaning: Dominoes
words.usage: Played in pairs at a table in the street, loudly, with a ring of advisers.

words.meaning: Baseball; literally, ball
words.usage: The national passion since the 1860s. Arguments about it in Havana’s Parque Central never end.

words.meaning: Friend; mate
words.usage: The everyday greeting between friends. The word came into street Spanish from the Abakuá brotherhoods.

words.meaning: Blessing; life force; good luck
words.usage: A word from Afro-Cuban religion that everyone uses: to have aché is to have grace.

words.meaning: A pleated shirt with four pockets, worn untucked
words.usage: Formal dress for a hot country. Said to come from Sancti Spíritus.

words.meaning: An old American car used as a shared taxi
words.usage: Literally a big almond. A 1950s body, kept going with whatever engine could be found.

words.meaning: A fighter in the wars of independence against Spain
words.usage: The barefoot cavalry of the nineteenth century, many of them formerly enslaved.

words.meaning: Great; cool
words.usage: General approval, for a person, a plan or a plate of food.

practices.name: Cafecito
practices.instructions: Make coffee the Cuban way in a stovetop pot. Put a spoonful of sugar in a cup. When the first dark drops come up, pour them onto the sugar and beat it with a spoon until it turns pale and thick. Pour in the rest of the coffee and stir, so that a light foam rises. Serve it in small cups. Take one to someone: a neighbour, a colleague, someone at home.
practices.why: In Cuba coffee is a gift passed from hand to hand. The pale foam, the espumita, is the pride of the maker, and a cup offered at the door is the first act of welcome.
variations: Make it for three people and drink it together.
Add a pinch of salt or a drop of milk.
Take a cup to the person next door.

practices.name: Greet the street
practices.instructions: On your way out, greet everyone you meet by name or with a nod, in the Cuban way: buenos días, a smile, a question after the family. Say it to the neighbour on the stairs, the person at the shop, the person on the bench. A street is a place where everybody knows everybody a little. Practise making it so.
practices.why: In Cuban neighbourhoods, a greeting is expected, and walking by without one is rude. The rule of this Onda is to greet everyone on your own street.
variations: Learn one new neighbour’s name.
Ask after someone’s mother.
Greet people in Spanish, if you can.

practices.name: A song with the dishes
practices.instructions: Put on a son or a bolero while you tidy the kitchen, wash the cups and make the bed. Sing along, badly. Move your hips a little as you carry things. In Cuba music is on while one works, from the radio, the neighbour or the street. The task goes faster and the house is warmer for it.
practices.why: Music on while you work is a Cuban rule. It takes the dullness out of morning chores and makes a house feel lived in.
variations: Use an old radio station.
Learn the chorus of one song.
Dance one step while the kettle boils.

practices.name: Fresh juice from what you have
practices.instructions: Squeeze juice from whatever fruit is in the house, orange, lime, grapefruit or guava, and drink it in a tall glass, with ice if it is hot. In Cuba fruit is served fresh, in a batido or a juice, and nothing is wasted. Drink it slowly at the window. If you have no fruit, cut one apple into neat slices and share it.
practices.why: Fresh fruit is part of everyday Cuban eating. The habit of using what you have, in a way that makes something small feel like a treat, is at the heart of the Onda.
variations: Make a batido with milk and banana.
Add mint and a pinch of sugar.
Share a glass with someone.

practices.name: Mend something small
practices.instructions: Choose one thing that is broken or loose: a button, a hinge, a torn bag, a wobbly chair. Spend ten minutes mending it with what you have. Use tape, glue, thread, a nail. In Cuba, things are fixed and fixed again, and fixing is a skill that people are proud of. Put it back in use right away.
practices.why: Mending before buying is one of the Onda’s rules. Decades of scarcity made Cuban repair and invention famous, and the pleasure of making a thing work again is universal.
variations: Fix something for a neighbour.
Learn a new repair from a video.
Make something useful from a jar or box.

practices.name: Open the windows and the day
practices.instructions: Open every shutter and window you can, let in the air and the street noise, and stand in the light for a few moments with a coffee. Cuban houses are built to breathe, with high ceilings and open doors. Greet the day the way you would greet a guest. If it is cold, open them for just two minutes and then close.
practices.why: Cuban houses are open to air and to street, with portales, porches, and wide doors. Letting the day in is a small pleasure that connects the inside to the outside.
variations: Sit on the front step for five minutes.
Water a plant while the window is open.
Wave to someone across the street.

practices.name: Find the clave
practices.instructions: Put on a son or a rumba: the Septeto Nacional, Arsenio Rodríguez, Los Muñequitos de Matanzas. Clap the clave, the five-stroke pattern that holds the music together. Count eight quick beats in a bar. In the first bar clap on one, on four and on seven. In the second bar clap on three and on five. Repeat without stopping. Keep it steady.
practices.why: Cuban music is built on the clave, a pattern that every instrument either plays or plays around. Once you can feel it, the music opens up.
variations: Clap it on two sticks or spoons.
Walk to the beat.
Clap it while someone else sings.

practices.name: Sobremesa
practices.instructions: After the main meal of the day, stay at the table for twenty minutes. Leave the plates where they are. Bring coffee or fruit. Keep phones out of sight. Talk, and let the talk go where it wants: a story, the news of the street, an old argument, a plan. If you eat alone, take the twenty minutes anyway with a coffee and a call to someone.
practices.why: The meal in a Cuban home does not end when the plates are empty. The time after is where the talk and the family happen, and it is what people remember.
variations: Play dominoes or cards at the table.
Tell the story of one of your elders.
Serve a small sweet with the coffee.

practices.name: Resolver
practices.instructions: Each day solve one small problem with what you already have. Mend the broken thing before you replace it. Cook from what is in the cupboard. Borrow the tool from next door and return it with something. Turn a jar into a lamp, a crate into a shelf, yesterday’s rice into today’s lunch. Keep a short note of what you resolved and how.
practices.why: Decades of shortages made resolver, to find a way, a national art. It is resourcefulness with humour, and it is a skill worth having anywhere.
variations: Solve a problem for someone else.
Make a tool from what is lying around.
Swap something you do not need for something you do.

practices.name: Slap down a domino
practices.instructions: Play dominoes with a neighbour, a friend or family, in pairs, as Cubans do on the street, on a card table in the shade. Slap each tile down with a flourish and talk loudly. Play a game to 100, or just for twenty minutes. Win with style and lose with a joke. If you have no one to play with, play against yourself.
practices.why: Dominoes is the game of the Cuban street and portal. The sound of tiles slapped on a table is a part of daily life.
variations: Play with a double-nine set.
Teach a child to play.
Play in the street, in front of your house.

practices.name: Dance a few bars of son
practices.instructions: Put on a son and learn the basic step: three steps in a box, back and forth, with a pause on the fourth beat. Move your hips gently and keep your shoulders still. Dance alone or with a partner. In Cuba the dance is learned by watching and doing, in the street and at parties. Ten minutes is enough to start.
practices.why: Son is the root of Cuban dance music, and its basic step is easy to pick up. Dancing it feels like joining a conversation.
variations: Follow a video lesson.
Dance with a neighbour or friend.
Dance one slow bolero with someone.

practices.name: Share what you have
practices.instructions: Give something to a neighbour or friend today: a bowl of fruit, a cup of rice, a jar of jam, a tool lent, an hour of help. Where one eats, two eat. Do not wait to be asked. It does not have to be much. Sharing is how people get through hard times in Cuba, and it is also how a street becomes a community.
practices.why: Where one eats, two eat is a Cuban rule. A culture of sharing sustained people through many shortages and made neighbourhoods strong.
variations: Share a meal with someone alone.
Lend something and do not ask for it back.
Leave a gift at a neighbour’s door.

practices.name: Take the evening air
practices.instructions: When the heat goes out of the day, go and sit where people pass: the front step, a balcony, a bench, the sea wall if you have one. Take a chair if you can. Greet everyone by name or with a nod. Let conversations start. Do not bring anything to do. On a wet evening, stand at an open window or door for ten minutes and then telephone someone.
practices.why: Sitting out in the evening on the portal, the porch, or along the Malecón is the heart of Cuban social life. It costs nothing and it is the best part of the day.
variations: Bring a stool and sit by the road.
Bring a flask of coffee for passers-by.
Listen to the street without a phone.

practices.name: Cook moros y cristianos
practices.instructions: Cook black beans with rice in one pot: sofrito of onion, green pepper and garlic, cumin, a bay leaf, and the beans and rice simmered together until the rice is swollen with the dark stock. Serve with a slice of lime and a spoon of oil. It is the daily plate and the meal that brings people to the table.
practices.why: Moros y cristianos, black beans and white rice together, is a basic Cuban dish. A pot of it feeds many people, and the smell of the sofrito brings the family into the kitchen.
variations: Make it with leftover rice.
Cook it and take a bowl next door.
Serve it with fried plantain.

practices.name: A décima by candlelight
practices.instructions: Write or read a décima, the ten-line verse of rural Cuba, with a rhyme scheme of ABBAACCDDC. Write ten lines about your day, a person you love or your street. Read it aloud, or sing it to a simple tune. Guajiros improvised décimas in contests called controversias. You do not have to be good. You have to be playful.
practices.why: The décima is the folk poem of Cuba, brought from Spain and made local. Improvising rhyme in front of friends is an old pleasure of the countryside.
variations: Write a décima with a friend, line by line.
Use a proverb as the last line.
Read a décima by a Cuban poet.

practices.name: The bolero hour
practices.instructions: Put on a bolero, such as Los Panchos, Olga Guillot or Beny Moré’s Como fue, and listen to the whole thing sitting down, with the lights low. Boleros are slow songs of love and longing, in Cuba since the 1880s. Sing along if you wish. It is a gentle, romantic end to the day.
practices.why: The bolero is Cuba’s slow love song. It has crossed the whole Spanish-speaking world, and it makes a quiet evening feel special.
variations: Dance a bolero slowly with a partner.
Learn the words of a chorus.
Listen with your eyes closed.

practices.name: A phone call to family
practices.instructions: Phone a relative or an old friend, especially one who lives far away, and have a proper talk of twenty minutes. Ask about their day, their health and their garden. In Cuban families, spread across the island and the world, phone calls are how the family is held together. Call someone without being asked.
practices.why: The Cuban family is spread between the island and the diaspora, and the regular call is a tie that holds it together.
variations: Call a grandparent.
Call someone you have not spoken to for a year.
Send a voice message to someone far away.

practices.name: Slow dancing in the kitchen
practices.instructions: Before bed, put on one slow song and dance in the kitchen or the living room with a partner, a child or alone. Hold on, sway and say nothing. A house in Cuba often has a radio on and someone swaying as they cook. It is a little act of closeness at the end of the day.
practices.why: Dancing at home, spontaneously, is part of everyday Cuban life. It turns the end of the day into something warm.
variations: Dance barefoot.
Dance with a child on your feet.
Dance alone and enjoy it.

practices.name: A domino afternoon on the street
practices.instructions: Set up a table in the shade, outside if you can, with a set of dominoes, a pot of coffee and a few friends or neighbours. Play in pairs for a couple of hours, trading jokes and gossip. Cuban streets have a table like this on almost every corner. Keep a tally on a bit of paper. Let someone new join the game.
practices.why: A domino table is the social centre of many Cuban neighbourhoods. Playing for the pleasure of company is the point.
variations: Hold a small tournament.
Play at a park table.
Bring a pot of coffee to share.

practices.name: A feast of ajiaco
practices.instructions: Cook a big pot of ajiaco, the stew of roots, corn, plantain and meat or beans that Fernando Ortiz used as an image of Cuba itself. Cassava, malanga, sweet potato, pumpkin and corn simmered together for hours. Invite friends, and let each bring an ingredient. Eat it all together, and talk about what is in it and where it came from.
practices.why: Ajiaco is a stew into which everything goes, and Ortiz used it as an image for Cuban culture, a mix that stays distinct yet becomes one. Cooking it with others is a good lesson.
variations: Ask each guest to bring an ingredient.
Make a vegetarian version.
Serve with lime and hot sauce.

immersePlan.name: Read Versos sencillos
immersePlan.text: Read five of José Martí’s simple verses, written in the Catskill Mountains by an exile homesick for Cuba. Read one aloud, slowly, and learn a line.

immersePlan.name: Read Motivos de son
immersePlan.text: Read poems by Nicolás Guillén that take the rhythm of son and the speech of the street. Read them aloud, with the beat.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Dreaming in Cuban
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Cristina García’s novel of three generations of women, split between Havana and Brooklyn. Notice the voices that speak.

immersePlan.name: Watch Buena Vista Social Club
immersePlan.text: Watch Wim Wenders’s film about a group of half-forgotten Cuban musicians in their seventies and eighties who record an album and go on tour. Watch the faces as they play.

immersePlan.name: Watch Chico and Rita
immersePlan.text: Watch the animated love story of a pianist and a singer, from Havana in the 1940s to New York. The music is the story. Sing along when you can.

immersePlan.name: Watch Strawberry and Chocolate
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1993 film about a friendship between a young student and a gay artist in Havana. Notice the humour, and what is said over ice cream.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Buena Vista album
immersePlan.text: Play the album recorded in six days in an old Havana studio, starting with Chan Chan. Hum the bassline.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Benny Moré
immersePlan.text: Play the greatest voice of Cuban popular music in front of the big band he led. Pick one song, listen twice and dance once.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Los Muñequitos de Matanzas
immersePlan.text: Play the rumba group who built their sound on drums and voices. Listen for the clave and the answering voices, and clap along.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Jungle
immersePlan.text: Look at Wifredo Lam’s painting where figures that are part human, part cane and part mask crowd a moonlit field. Decide what each figure is.

immersePlan.name: Look at Gitana tropical
immersePlan.text: Look at Víctor Manuel’s 1929 portrait of a calm young woman against a tropical landscape, often called the Mona Lisa of Cuba. Look at her eyes.

immersePlan.name: Look at Fusterlandia
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the tile-covered houses and streets of a Havana neighbourhood, made by the artist José Fuster. Pick the corner you would sit on.

immersePlan.name: Cook moros y cristianos
immersePlan.text: Cook black beans and rice together in one pot, with a sofrito of onion, pepper and garlic. Serve it with a slice of lime and share a bowl.

immersePlan.name: Make tostones
immersePlan.text: Cut green plantains into thick slices, fry once, squash flat, and fry again until golden. Salt them and eat them hot with garlic sauce.

immersePlan.name: Eat guava with white cheese
immersePlan.text: Eat a slice of guava paste on a slice of fresh white cheese, the classic simple dessert. Notice how sweet and salty meet.

immersePlan.name: Make a café cubano
immersePlan.text: Beat the first dark drops of coffee with sugar until pale and thick, and pour in the rest. Serve in small cups and share one.

immersePlan.name: Make a batido
immersePlan.text: Blend a fruit with milk and ice: mamey, mango, guava or banana. Drink it cold with a straw and a friend.

immersePlan.name: Drink fresh sugar cane juice
immersePlan.text: Drink cold sugar cane juice, pressed while you wait, if you can find it. If not, drink a glass of cold sweet fruit juice slowly in the shade.

immersePlan.name: Be the reader in the factory
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter aloud to someone while they work or cook. Since 1865 cigar rollers have paid one of their number to read to them. Choose a chapter that makes them laugh.

immersePlan.name: Play dominoes in the street
immersePlan.text: Play dominoes with a neighbour at a table outside. Slap the tiles down with a flourish and tell stories between hands.

immersePlan.name: Greet an elder with respect
immersePlan.text: Greet your parents, grandparents or an elder with respect and ask for their blessing, as children do in Cuban families. Say it warmly and listen to the reply.

immersePlan.name: Play dominó
immersePlan.text: Play with a double-nine set of fifty-five tiles in two pairs. Count points to 100 and slap the tiles on the table.

immersePlan.name: Play pelota
immersePlan.text: Play or watch baseball, Cuba’s national game, first recorded at Palmar de Junco in 1874. Throw a ball back and forth with someone for ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Play chess after Capablanca
immersePlan.text: Play a short game of chess, in the manner of José Raúl Capablanca, who learned at four and became world champion. Aim for clarity, not tricks.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Carnival of Santiago
immersePlan.text: Look at photographs and videos of the oldest and loudest carnival on the island, held in late July with neighbourhood comparsas parading. Pick your favourite drum.

immersePlan.name: Walk through Old Havana in pictures
immersePlan.text: Look at photographs of the five squares, baroque churches and streets of balconies, founded in 1519. Pick a balcony and imagine the view.

immersePlan.name: Visit the Casa de la Trova in Santiago
immersePlan.text: Look up the small room open to the street where musicians play son every day. Listen to a video of a session.

immersePlan.name: Learn resolver
immersePlan.text: Resolver means to solve, to get by. Find one small problem today and solve it with what you already have.

immersePlan.name: Learn sobremesa
immersePlan.text: Sobremesa is the time at the table after the meal. Stay for twenty minutes today after one meal and talk.

immersePlan.name: Learn clave
immersePlan.text: Clave is the key rhythm of Cuban music. Clap it with a record for two minutes and feel it settle.

rules.text: Greet everyone on your own street
rules.why: In a Cuban neighbourhood no one passes in silence. Good morning to every person between your door and the corner, every time.
Resolver comes first. Nothing new enters the house today until you have tried to fix, borrow or adapt.
The saying goes: donde come uno, comen dos. Whatever you cook today, there is enough for whoever turns up.
Cooking, cleaning and repairs are done to a radio. Put on a son or a bolero for at least one chore, and move to it.
Do not be the first to get up. Give the sobremesa twenty minutes after the last mouthful.

rules.text: A good face for bad weather
rules.why: Al mal tiempo, buena cara. Complain once, make a joke of it and get on with finding a way.

read.title: Versos sencillos
read.creator: José Martí
read.why: Forty-six short poems written in the Catskill Mountains by an exile homesick for the island. Every Cuban knows some by heart, and one became the words of Guantanamera.

read.title: Cuban Counterpoint: Tobacco and Sugar
read.creator: Fernando Ortiz
read.why: The founding book of Cuban self-understanding. He sets the two great crops against each other like characters, and coins the word transculturation.

read.title: Biography of a Runaway Slave
read.creator: Miguel Barnet, from the words of Esteban Montejo
read.why: A man of 103 recalls slavery, years hidden in the forest and the war of independence.

read.title: Cecilia Valdés
read.creator: Cirilo Villaverde
read.why: The great Cuban novel of the nineteenth century: love, colour and slavery in the Havana of the 1830s.

read.title: Motivos de son
read.creator: Nicolás Guillén
read.why: Eight poems in the speech and rhythm of Black Havana. They caused a scandal and changed Spanish-language poetry.

read.title: The Old Man and the Sea
read.creator: Ernest Hemingway
read.why: Written at his house outside Havana about a fisherman from Cojímar. Short enough for one sitting.

read.title: Cuba: An American History
read.creator: Ada Ferrer
read.why: Five centuries of the island and its tangled life with the United States, by a historian born in Havana.

read.title: Dreaming in Cuban
read.creator: Cristina García
read.why: Three generations of women divided between Havana and Brooklyn. A novel of the diaspora.

watch.title: Buena Vista Social Club
watch.creator: Wim Wenders
watch.why: A group of half-forgotten musicians in their seventies and eighties record an album and play Carnegie Hall. Watch their faces.

watch.title: Memories of Underdevelopment
watch.creator: Tomás Gutiérrez Alea
watch.why: A well-off writer stays behind when his family leaves for Miami and watches Havana change around him. The classic of Cuban cinema.

watch.title: Strawberry and Chocolate
watch.creator: Tomás Gutiérrez Alea and Juan Carlos Tabío
watch.why: A friendship between a young Communist student and a gay artist in 1970s Havana. Funny, brave and full of the city.

watch.title: Chico and Rita
watch.creator: Fernando Trueba and Javier Mariscal
watch.why: An animated love story between a pianist and a singer, from Havana in 1948 to New York, with a great score.

watch.title: Vampires in Havana
watch.creator: Juan Padrón
watch.why: A cartoon comedy about a trumpet player who does not know he is a vampire, set in the 1930s. A cult favourite on the island.

watch.title: I Am Cuba
watch.creator: Mikhail Kalatozov
watch.why: A Soviet-Cuban production with some of the most astonishing camera movements ever filmed. Propaganda, and unforgettable to look at.

listen.title: Buena Vista Social Club
listen.creator: Buena Vista Social Club
listen.why: Recorded in six days in an old Havana studio. Start with Chan Chan and Dos gardenias.

listen.title: Son de la loma
listen.creator: Trío Matamoros
listen.why: They are from the hills and they sing on the plain. One of the first sones the whole island sang.

listen.title: Benny Moré with his Banda Gigante
listen.creator: Benny Moré
listen.why: The greatest voice of Cuban popular music, in front of a big band he led without being able to read a note.

listen.title: Guantanamera
listen.creator: Joseíto Fernández, with verses by José Martí
listen.why: A country tune that a radio singer used for the day’s news in the 1930s, later joined to Martí’s Simple Verses.

listen.title: Los Muñequitos de Matanzas
listen.creator: Rumba
listen.why: The leading rumba group. Three drums, sticks, a lead singer and a chorus, and nothing else.

listen.title: La Comparsa
listen.creator: Ernesto Lecuona
listen.why: A piano piece in which a carnival band approaches from far off, passes and fades. He wrote it at seventeen.

listen.title: Celia Cruz with La Sonora Matancera
listen.creator: Celia Cruz
listen.why: The Havana recordings that made her the queen of the music, before she left the island in 1960.

art.title: The Jungle
art.creator: Wifredo Lam
art.why: Figures that are part human, part sugar cane and part mask crowd a moonlit thicket. Painted on his return to Cuba from Europe. Museum of Modern Art, New York.

art.title: Gitana tropical
art.creator: Víctor Manuel
art.why: A calm young woman against a tropical landscape, often called the Mona Lisa of Cuban painting. Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, Havana.

art.title: Still lifes and the Habana Libre mural
art.creator: Amelia Peláez
art.why: Fruit, fish and flowers held inside thick black lines like the stained glass of old Havana houses, and a vast mosaic on a hotel front.

art.title: Havana fanlights
art.creator: Coloured glass above doors and windows
art.why: Half-wheels of red, blue and yellow glass that break the hard sun into colour on the floor. The plainest sign of a Havana house.

art.title: Fusterlandia
art.creator: José Fuster
art.why: An artist covered his own house in mosaic and then, with their agreement, the houses of his neighbours. Jaimanitas, Havana.

eat.title: Moros y cristianos
eat.creator: Black beans and rice cooked together
eat.why: The daily plate. The beans are simmered with a sofrito of onion, garlic, pepper, cumin and bay.

eat.title: Ropa vieja
eat.creator: Shredded beef stewed with tomato and peppers
eat.why: The name means old clothes. It came from the Canary Islands and became a national dish.

eat.title: Ajiaco
eat.creator: A stew of roots, corn, plantain and several meats
eat.why: Cassava, malanga, sweet potato and yam cooked for hours. The dish Ortiz took as the picture of Cuba.

eat.title: Lechón asado with yuca
eat.creator: Roast pork with garlic and sour orange, and boiled cassava
eat.why: The meal of Christmas Eve, cooked outdoors for the whole family and half the street.

eat.title: Tostones
eat.creator: Green plantain, fried, flattened and fried again
eat.why: Salted and eaten hot. Ripe plantain fried soft and sweet is their opposite number.

eat.title: Guava with white cheese
eat.creator: A slice of each
eat.why: The simplest dessert on the island, in a pastry or on a plate.

drink.title: Café cubano
drink.creator: Strong coffee beaten with sugar
drink.why: Small, dark and sweet, with a pale foam on top. Made to be shared.

drink.title: Guarapo
drink.creator: Fresh sugar cane juice over ice
drink.why: Pressed while you wait. Grassy, sweet and cold.

drink.title: Batido
drink.creator: A fruit milkshake
drink.why: Mamey, mango, guava or banana, blended with milk and ice.

drink.title: Mojito
drink.creator: Mint, lime, sugar and soda water, with or without rum
drink.why: Crush the mint gently with the sugar and lime. Without the rum it is still a very good drink.

customs.title: The reader in the factory
customs.creator: A voice over the workbenches
customs.why: Since 1865 cigar rollers have paid one of their number to read to them: the newspapers in the morning and a novel in the afternoon. Some cigars are named after the books they liked.

customs.title: Asking a blessing
customs.creator: A greeting to elders
customs.why: Children and grown children greet parents, grandparents and godparents by asking for their blessing, and are answered: God bless you.

customs.title: Burning the old year
customs.creator: Midnight on 31 December
customs.why: A rag doll that stands for the year’s troubles is set alight, and a bucket of water is thrown out of the front door to carry them off.

customs.title: Dominoes in the street
customs.creator: A table, four chairs and an audience
customs.why: Tiles are slapped down hard, and commentary from the onlookers is part of the game.

customs.title: The fifteenth birthday
customs.creator: Los quince
customs.why: A girl’s coming of age, marked with a dress, a party, a waltz and a book of photographs that families save up for.

games.title: Dominó
games.creator: Tile game · Cuba
games.why: Havana plays with a double-nine set of fifty-five tiles, in two pairs. You may not speak to your partner about the game, so everything is said with the tiles.

games.title: Pelota
games.creator: Baseball · Cuba
games.why: The first recorded game on the island was played at Palmar de Junco in Matanzas in 1874. Children play a street version called four corners with a stick and a bottle cap.

games.title: Chess, after Capablanca
games.creator: Board game
games.why: José Raúl Capablanca learned the game at four by watching his father and went eight years without losing. Play through one of his endgames.

games.title: Santiago de Cuba
games.creator: Board game · Michael Rieneck
games.why: Drive a car round the city, calling on a tobacco grower, a musician and a rum maker, and load the ships in the harbour. Light and quick.

games.title: Tropico 6
games.creator: Video game · Limbic Entertainment
games.why: A comic strategy game about ruling a Caribbean island, with a score by Cuban-style bands. It is a caricature, and it knows it.

festivals.title: Carnival of Santiago de Cuba
festivals.creator: Late July
festivals.why: The oldest and loudest on the island. Neighbourhood comparsas parade behind drums and the wail of the Chinese cornet.

festivals.title: Parrandas de Remedios
festivals.creator: 24 December, Remedios
festivals.why: Two halves of a small town compete all night with floats, lanterns and fireworks. Recognised by UNESCO in 2018.

festivals.title: Havana Jazz Festival
festivals.creator: January
festivals.why: Founded in 1980. Cuban and visiting musicians play in theatres and clubs across the city.

festivals.title: Romerías de Mayo
festivals.creator: Early May, Holguín
festivals.why: Young artists from many countries fill the town for a week that starts with a walk up the Hill of the Cross.

festivals.title: Christmas Eve
festivals.creator: 24 December
festivals.why: Nochebuena: the whole family at one long table for roast pork, beans, cassava and music.

festivals.title: Day of Cuban Culture
festivals.creator: 20 October
festivals.why: The anniversary of the first singing of the national anthem, in Bayamo in 1868.

places.title: Old Havana
places.creator: Havana, Cuba
places.why: Five squares, baroque churches and streets of balconies, founded in 1519. A World Heritage Site and a lived-in neighbourhood.

places.title: Viñales Valley
places.creator: Pinar del Río, Cuba
places.why: Red earth, tobacco fields worked with oxen and limestone hills that rise like haystacks. Farmers show visitors how leaves are dried and rolled.

places.title: Trinidad
places.creator: Sancti Spíritus, Cuba
places.why: A sugar town of cobbled streets and pastel houses, with the valley of the old mills below. The fortunes were made by enslaved labour.

places.title: Casa de la Trova
places.creator: Santiago de Cuba
places.why: A small room open to the street where the old songs have been played every day for decades.

places.title: Matanzas
places.creator: Matanzas, Cuba
places.why: The city of bridges where the danzón was first played and rumba grew up among the dockworkers.

places.title: Callejón de Hamel
places.creator: Centro Habana, Cuba
places.why: An alley covered in murals by Salvador González, with rumba played in the open on Sundays.

places.title: Calle Ocho
places.creator: Little Havana, Miami, USA
places.why: The main street of the Cuban diaspora: coffee windows, cigar rollers and the old men at Domino Park.

places.title: Ybor City
places.creator: Tampa, Florida, USA
places.why: The cigar town built by Cuban, Spanish and Italian workers in the 1880s, where Martí came to raise money and the readers read.

ethics.title: Where one eats, two eat
ethics.text: Food is shared with whoever is there, and a visitor is never asked whether they have eaten: a plate is put in front of them. With ration books and shortages, this has not been a small thing.
ethics.practice: Cook more than you need today and take a plate to someone.

ethics.title: The neighbour comes first
ethics.text: When something breaks or runs out, the first call is next door. Tools, sugar, medicine and news move along the street. What you lend comes back in another form.
ethics.practice: Ask a neighbour for a small favour today, and offer one.

ethics.title: Respect for elders
ethics.text: Grandparents live in the house and are greeted first. Children ask for their blessing. An old person’s story is not interrupted.
ethics.practice: Greet the oldest person you meet today before anyone else, and ask them something.

ethics.title: Dignity in making do
ethics.text: To resolve is to refuse to be beaten by lack. It asks for patience, wit and pride in the workmanship. It should not be romanticised: people would rather have had the spare part.
ethics.practice: Do one repair today properly, so that it will last.

ethics.title: Laughing at power
ethics.text: Cubans call it choteo: the habit of taking nothing solemnly and deflating anyone who puts on airs. The essayist Jorge Mañach studied it in 1928 as both a weakness and a defence.
ethics.practice: Find the joke in something that is weighing on you, and tell it to someone.

ethics.title: Pride in craft
ethics.text: A cigar roller, a tres player and a mechanic who keeps a 1952 Chevrolet running are all masters, and are spoken of as such. Doing a thing well is its own standing.
ethics.practice: Do one ordinary task today as a craftsman would.

philosophy.title: Transculturation
philosophy.text: Fernando Ortiz coined the word in 1940. When peoples meet, he argued, neither side simply takes on the other’s ways. Both lose something and both are changed, and something new is born that did not exist before. Cuba is his example.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing in your life that exists only because two traditions met.

philosophy.title: The ajiaco
philosophy.text: Ortiz’s image for the nation is a stew that never leaves the fire. Taíno roots, Spanish meat, African yams and Chinese spice go in at different times and cook at different rates. The broth at the bottom is thick and blended, and what went in last is still whole on top.
philosophy.practice: List the ingredients of your own stew: places, languages, people. Which are fully cooked and which are still whole?

philosophy.title: Homeland is humanity
philosophy.text: José Martí spent most of his adult life in exile, organising a war of independence that he hoped would be free of hatred. He wrote that the homeland is that part of humanity we see most closely and into which we happened to be born.
philosophy.practice: Do something today for the part of humanity nearest to you.

philosophy.title: Our America
philosophy.text: In an essay of 1891 Martí told the young republics of Latin America to stop copying Europe and the United States and to study their own lands and peoples. Graft the world onto our republics, he wrote, but let the trunk be our own.
philosophy.practice: Take one idea you have borrowed and ask whether it fits the ground you actually stand on.

philosophy.title: The marvellous real
philosophy.text: The novelist Alejo Carpentier argued in 1949 that in the Caribbean the marvellous does not have to be invented, as it was by the surrealists in Paris. It is found in the history and the daily life of the place.
philosophy.practice: Write down the most improbable true thing you saw today.

philosophy.title: Time at the table
philosophy.text: The sobremesa and the evening on the porch treat unhurried talk as a good in itself. Time spent with people is not thought of as lost.
philosophy.practice: Give someone an hour today without looking at a clock.

philosophy.title: Call and response
philosophy.text: In the montuno a singer throws out a line and the chorus throws it back, again and again, while each player varies his part inside the clave. The music is a model of how to be one voice among many.
philosophy.practice: In your next group conversation, answer what was actually said before adding your own line.

philosophy.title: There is always a way
philosophy.text: Resolver and inventar rest on a belief that no problem is final. It is practical optimism, held without illusions and usually with a joke.
philosophy.practice: Take one problem you have called impossible and list three imperfect ways through it.

journal: Whom did you greet today, and who greeted you?
Who drank coffee with you?
What did you resolve today, and with what?
How long did you stay at the table, and what was said?
What music was playing while you worked?
What is in your ajiaco?
Who came to the door, and what did you offer?
What did you borrow, and what did you lend?
What did you see from the front step this evening?
Where did you find the clave today, and where did you lose it?
What made you laugh at something serious?
Whose blessing would you ask?
What did you mend instead of replace?
What story did an older person tell you?
What did you cook, and who ate it?
What is the most improbable true thing you saw today?
Which neighbour do you still not know by name?
What did you do today with real craft?
What do you miss about a place you have left?
What was the bad weather today, and what face did you put on it?
When did you dance, or want to?
What have two different traditions made in you that neither had alone?
What did you do slowly that you usually rush?
What would you carry with you if you had to leave?
Who is your street, and what do you owe it?
Which borrowed idea does not fit your ground?
What did you give away today?
What song is stuck in your head, and where is it from?
What looked impossible this morning and was done by night?
For whom do you grow a white rose?
reflect: What changed when you greeted everyone on your street?
What did you mend or invent that you are proud of?
What happened at the table after the plates were empty?
What did holding the clave teach you about listening?
What have you learned about what you are made of?
Which habit will stay in your house?
dayThemes: Good morning to the whole street
A good face for bad weather
Those who left and those who stayed

intro: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, long and narrow, a hundred and fifty kilometres south of Florida. Its culture is one of the most recognisable on earth and one of the most mixed. Out of the meeting of Spanish settlers, enslaved Africans, the island’s first peoples and later arrivals from China, Haiti and elsewhere came a music the whole world dances to, a cuisine of rice, beans and pork, a way of talking with the whole body and a gift for getting by. This Onda is about that everyday culture: how Cubans live with one another.

The Spanish arrived with Columbus in 1492 and within decades the Taíno people had been all but destroyed by violence and disease, leaving words, foods and blood lines behind. For three centuries the island was a staging post for the treasure fleets. Then came sugar. From the late eighteenth century Cuba became the richest colony in the world and one of the cruellest, as hundreds of thousands of Africans were brought in chains to cut cane. Slavery lasted until 1886. The Yoruba, Kongo, Carabalí and other peoples carried their religions, drums and languages with them and kept them alive in mutual aid societies and in the courtyards of the poor.

Cuban culture grew where those worlds touched. The son, born in the eastern mountains, set a Spanish guitar over an African pulse. Rumba grew up among dockworkers in Havana and Matanzas. Catholic saints and African orishas came to share altars. The scholar Fernando Ortiz gave this process a name, transculturation, and gave the country its favourite image of itself: an ajiaco, a stew in which everything keeps cooking together.

The island won independence from Spain in 1898 after thirty years of war inspired by the poet José Martí, and then lived for six decades in the shadow of the United States. The revolution of 1959 brought free schools and clinics, a one-party state and a rupture with Washington that has lasted ever since. More than two million Cubans now live abroad. The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 began years of severe shortage. Through all of it, daily life has depended on the neighbour, the extended family and the ability to resolve.

Cubans disagree deeply about their government, and families are divided by the sea and by politics. This Onda takes no side in that argument. It is concerned with what people on the island and off it share: the first coffee offered to a visitor, the long talk after a meal, the evening on the porch, the rhythm called the clave, the repair that should not have worked.

You will make and share coffee each morning, learn to clap the clave, stay at the table, fix one thing a day and take the evening air. The Afro-Cuban religions are described here with respect and are not offered as practices. They are entered through initiation, under the guidance of their own elders.
guide.origin: The island of Cuba, and Cuban communities abroad, above all in Florida
guide.era: A living culture, shaped since the sixteenth century by Taíno, Spanish, African and Chinese inheritances

figures.name: José Martí
figures.bio: Poet, journalist and organiser of the last war of independence. Exiled at seventeen, he wrote and raised funds in New York for fifteen years, and was killed in his first battle. Every side of every Cuban argument claims him.

figures.name: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes
figures.bio: A planter who freed the people he had enslaved on 10 October 1868 and called on them to join him in fighting Spain. Known as the Father of the Homeland.

figures.name: Antonio Maceo
figures.bio: The Bronze Titan: a mule driver’s son of mixed descent who rose to second in command of the liberation army and was wounded more than twenty times.

figures.name: Mariana Grajales
figures.bio: Mother of Antonio Maceo. She ran field hospitals during the first war and sent all her sons to fight. Honoured as the mother of the nation.

figures.name: Fernando Ortiz
figures.bio: Lawyer turned anthropologist who spent sixty years studying Afro-Cuban music, religion and language and argued that they are the heart of Cuban culture. Called the third discoverer of Cuba.

figures.name: Lydia Cabrera
figures.bio: Writer who recorded the stories, plant lore and beliefs of Afro-Cuban elders in El Monte, published in 1954. She left the island in 1960.

figures.name: Nicolás Guillén
figures.bio: Poet from Camagüey who brought the rhythm of the son and the speech of Black Cubans into literature.

figures.name: Alejo Carpentier
figures.bio: Novelist and historian of Cuban music whose idea of the marvellous real shaped Latin American fiction.

figures.name: Ernesto Lecuona
figures.bio: Pianist and composer of more than six hundred pieces, among them Siboney and Malagueña. The most played Cuban composer.

figures.name: Arsenio Rodríguez
figures.bio: Blind player of the tres, descended from Kongo people, who added congas, piano and trumpets to the son band and laid the ground for salsa.

figures.name: Benny Moré
figures.bio: Singer from a village in Cienfuegos, known as the Barbarian of Rhythm, at home in every Cuban style.

figures.name: Celia Cruz
figures.bio: Singer from a poor district of Havana who became the best-known voice of Cuban music in the world. She left in 1960 and was never allowed to return.

figures.name: José Raúl Capablanca
figures.bio: World chess champion from 1921 to 1927, admired for the clarity of his play. Cuba’s first global celebrity.

figures.name: Wifredo Lam
figures.bio: Painter of Chinese, African and Spanish descent who worked alongside Picasso in Paris and then turned Afro-Cuban imagery into modern art.

figures.name: Alicia Alonso
figures.bio: Ballerina who danced for decades while nearly blind and founded the company that became the National Ballet of Cuba.

history.detail: Taíno farmers and older groups of fishers and gatherers lived across the island. They grew cassava, maize and tobacco and slept in hammocks. All four words come from their language.

He came ashore on the north-east coast and wrote that it was the most beautiful land human eyes had seen. Conquest followed from 1511, led by Diego Velázquez. The chief Hatuey, who resisted, was burned at the stake.
The town was moved to its present site beside a deep, sheltered bay. It became the gathering point for Spain’s treasure fleets and one of the most heavily fortified ports in the Americas.
They held the city for eleven months and opened it to trade. When Spain got it back, the island’s economy began to shift toward sugar and enslaved labour on a large scale.

Revolution in neighbouring Haiti ended production there. Cuba took its place. Over the next seventy years several hundred thousand Africans were brought to the island, and planters fleeing Haiti started coffee farms in the east.
Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed those he held in slavery and declared independence. The Ten Years’ War that followed failed, and it made a nation of people who had fought side by side.
Spain abolished slavery in Cuba, later than anywhere in the Americas except Brazil.
Three months after launching the final war of independence, José Martí rode into a Spanish ambush at Dos Ríos and was killed.
The United States entered the war after the battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour. Spain gave up the island. A republic was declared on 20 May 1902, under a clause that let Washington intervene.

The music of the east reached the capital and was taken up by sextets and septets. Radio began in 1922. In 1930 a recording of The Peanut Vendor made in New York started a worldwide craze for Cuban rhythm.
A progressive constitution was adopted. In the same year Fernando Ortiz published Cuban Counterpoint.

The dictator Fulgencio Batista fled and the rebel movement led by Fidel Castro took power. Land and businesses were nationalised and a one-party socialist state followed. Hundreds of thousands left, most for Florida.

A national campaign sent young volunteers to teach the countryside to read. The United States imposed a trade embargo that is still in force. In October 1962 the island was at the centre of the nuclear crisis between Washington and Moscow.
The Soviet Union collapsed and with it most of Cuba’s trade. Fuel, food and electricity ran short for years. People planted city gardens, rode bicycles and learned to mend everything.
An album by veteran musicians, recorded in Havana, sold millions and reminded the world of the old son.
UNESCO added Cuban rumba to its list of the intangible heritage of humanity. The country singing called punto followed in 2017.

concepts.text: The root of Cuban popular music.
concepts.detail: It took shape in the mountains of Oriente in the late nineteenth century: a tres guitar, a bass, bongos, maracas, claves and voices. A sung verse leads into the montuno, where soloist and chorus answer each other. Mambo, cha-cha-chá and salsa all grow from it.

A pattern of five strokes spread unevenly across two bars, with three on one side and two on the other. It comes from West and Central African timelines. Musicians do not so much play it as play inside it, and dancers feel it even when no one is striking the sticks.

A secular tradition of drumming, singing and dance created by Black workers in the ports. It has three forms: the slow yambú, the flirtatious guaguancó and the fast, acrobatic columbia, danced by men.

Ortiz’s term of 1940, offered as a correction to the idea that one culture simply absorbs another. In Cuba, he argued, every group was uprooted and every group was changed, and Cuban culture is the result.
The everyday practice of solving problems of supply through repair, substitution, barter and favours. It depends on knowing people. It is spoken of with pride and with weariness.

Ortiz set them against each other. Tobacco is native, grown on small farms by free men and worked by hand with skill. Sugar is foreign, grown on vast estates by enslaved people and processed by machine. The island’s history is their argument.

Cigar rolling is quiet work, and from 1865 the workers hired readers. They heard the news, political essays, Hugo, Dumas and Cervantes. Cigar workers became the best-informed trade on the island and the backbone of the independence movement in exile.
Country singers improvise ten-line stanzas over a small guitar, often in contest. The form came from Spain in the sixteenth century and was kept up by farmers of Canary Island descent.

Regla de Ocha, widely called Santería, honours the orishas of the Yoruba, who are paired with Catholic saints. Palo has Kongo roots, and Abakuá is a brotherhood from the Cross River region. They are living, initiatory religions with their own priests, and they have given Cuban music many of its rhythms and words.

More than two million Cubans live abroad, the largest number in and around Miami. They have kept the food, the music, the coffee windows and the dominoes, and changed them. Cuban culture today is made on both sides of the water.

facts.text: Two famous cigar brands, Montecristo and Romeo y Julieta, take their names from novels and plays that factory readers read aloud.
The bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world, lives only in Cuba. It weighs less than two grams.
Cuba had a working railway in 1837, more than ten years before Spain did.
The words hammock, canoe, tobacco, barbecue and hurricane all came into European languages from Taíno.
The national bird, the tocororo, has red, white and blue feathers, the colours of the flag.
José Raúl Capablanca did not lose a single tournament or match game between 1916 and 1924.
The daiquiri is named after a beach and iron mine near Santiago de Cuba, where an American engineer is said to have mixed the first one around 1898.

sensitivity.note: This Onda draws on the everyday culture of a living people, on the island and in the diaspora, who disagree strongly about their country’s politics. It takes no side. It also describes skills that grew out of real hardship, and religions that are entered only through initiation. It treats the first with respect and does not offer the second as practices.
requiredCaveats: Making do is admired in Cuba and was not chosen. Shortage, power cuts and emigration are painful facts and should not be treated as charming.
Cubans on and off the island hold strong and differing views of the revolution and the government. Nothing here endorses or condemns either position.
Regla de Ocha, Palo and Abakuá are initiatory religions. They are described here and never imitated.
Rum and cigars are part of the island’s history. Nothing in this Onda asks you to drink or smoke, and tobacco harms health.
This content has not yet been reviewed by Cuban cultural bearers or scholars. It should be before release.
